I find roguelikes to be extremely lazy design, because it's basically carte blanche to make an absurdly unbalanced, unfair and broken game and just say "Dying is part of the game, haha!".

There is a problem in RPGs with choice and consequence because of the possible consequences the game can enact on a player:

  1. The game will never kill you. This leads to a game where people make every choice as though they will come out on top in a fight.

  2. The game will kill you, but let you load. This leads to a game where you just memorize what actions get you through by trial and error.

  3. The game will impose some other lasting penalty on you. (Like, kill your favourite NPC) This is effective at raising the stakes, but still leaves you playing a superhero.

  4. The game will kill you and force you to start over. This leads to a game where prolonged adventures are all but impossible.

Roguelikes simply go with answer #4 and get around the problem that poses by not having a long and satisfying story to them. From my perspective that just doesn't quite get me to a point where I'm enjoying the fact that I'm not playing an invincible superhero but I still get a cool story.

What about the game like FTL: fast than light? There is nothing stopping you from winning in the first go, except inexperience. Each death is learning how to play the game better, but if you did a shit ton of research in theory you can beat it in one go. This is unlike rogue legacy where you are meant to go in and die multiple times, but each time you can upgrade and change classes (due to currency build from last run). My assumption is that the market is flooded with okay rogue-lite/rogues-like that it's making the genre look less appealing. There are definitely some great ones in the mix.

I own both FTL and Rogue Legacy and I agree that FTL is significantly nicer because it doesn't make you feel like you are meant to die over and over, but instead is just difficult to beat. I still think FTL has a bit too much random stuff going on where luck has a bigger impact on your ability to win than anything you actually do.

Overall, FTL isn't a bad game, but that's just where my personal taste kicks in and says I would much rather be playing the continuous space adventures of the USS Doesn't Blow Up than the dozens of tragic alternate reality deaths of the Kestel.
